item.title: HDFC Bank launches flexible EV car loan with longer battery repayment
item.description: The Flexi Electric Car Loan offers separate financing for the vehicle body and battery, allowing customers to customise EMIs and repay the battery portion over a longer tenure ...
item.dc:creator: Our Bureau
item.content:encoded: HDFC Bank, India’s largest private sector lender, on Sunday said it had launched the “Flexi Electric Car Loan”, which finances the body and battery of an electric vehicle (EV) in different proportions and allows the battery portion to be repaid over a longer term. The bank described the product as the first of its kind and said the structure allows customers to customise their equated monthly instalment (EMI) outflow. Batteries are the costliest component of an EV, making these vehicles more expensive to acquire than internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles, the bank said. The EMI on the battery portion will be comparable to the running cost of an ICE vehicle, it said, adding that the approach aligns with evolving battery subscription models. The loan is meant only for EV purchases and covers vehicles from leading original equipment manufacturers (OEMs). It is available at the bank’s more than 9,700 branches. “The EV revolution in India is fast gaining momentum, supported by government incentives, a push for an improved technological landscape and judicious policies. HDFC Bank’s Flexi Electric Car Loan is one more step in that direction as India is set to embrace the EV revolution. Further, we believe the Flexi Electric Car Loan will play a pivotal role in making EV ownership a cost-effective, seamless and hassle-free journey,” said Arvind Vohra, group head, retail assets and rural banking, HDFC Bank.

item.title: Rupee's recovery faces hurdles from dollar demand, capital outflows
item.description: The rupee's weakness is being driven by more than the West Asia conflict and elevated crude oil prices, with rising global borrowing costs, changes in importer and exporter hedging behaviour, and ...
item.dc:creator: Anjali Kumari
item.content:encoded: There is more to it in the rupee weakness than the West Asia conflict and elevated crude oil prices alone. The rising global borrowing costs, changes in importer and exporter hedging behaviour, and capital outflows have added to the pressure on the domestic currency. The rupee has appreciated 0.93 per cent in October so far, but has depreciated 0.14 per cent in the current financial year. The recent recovery proved short-lived, with the currency ending an eight-session winning streak on Thursday as rising crude oil prices amid tensions in West Asia renewed pressure. The rupee extended its losses on Friday to close at 94.94 per dollar, against 94.83 in the previous session. The currency had risen from 96.73 per dollar on October 9, close to its all-time low of 96.96 touched in May, to an intraday high of 94.33, aided by dollar inflows linked to the Jio Platforms initial public offering (IPO). However, the gains came amid active intervention by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in the spot and non-deliverable forwards markets. The RBI’s foreign exchange reserves fell by $5.01 billion to $721.02 billion in the week ended October 16. State-owned banks were also buying dollars for oil companies on the central bank’s behalf. The RBI has rolled out several measures to ease pressure on the currency. These include a special dollar window, operational from October 12, to meet the daily dollar requirements of Indian Oil Corporation, Bharat Petroleum Corporation and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation through designated banks. The central bank also tightened rules for banks’ foreign exchange derivative positions and opened concessional swap windows linked to foreign currency non-resident (bank) deposits, overseas foreign currency borrowings and external commercial borrowings. The RBI also raised the repo rate by 25 basis points (bps) to 5.5 per cent on October 7. However, the pressure on the rupee reflects broader shifts in global capital flows and domestic hedging behaviour. Expansionary fiscal policies and an artificial intelligence (AI)-led investment boom in the US have increased competition for capital, pushing up global borrowing costs. “The pressure on the rupee is led by elevated global bond yields, surge in crude oil prices and lately focus on AI-related investments,” said Gaura Sen Gupta, chief economist at IDFC FIRST Bank. The pressure is not limited to India, as the rising cost of capital is affecting emerging markets more broadly, she said. Domestically, expectations of further rupee depreciation have prompted importers to hedge their dollar payables, while exporters have held back from hedging their dollar receipts. This has increased demand for dollars in the market. The RBI’s foreign exchange risk reserve (FERR) framework seeks to address pressures arising from hedging activity. Dislocations in the forward market have added to volatility. Abhishek Goenka, founder and chief executive officer (CEO) of IFA Global, said dollar flows linked to the Jio Platforms IPO and associated funding swaps had widened the basis between spot and forward exchange rates. “Investors sell dollars in cash to subscribe to the IPO and book a forward to hedge currency risk,” Goenka said. These transactions, alongside the RBI’s sell-buy swaps to absorb surplus rupee liquidity from the banking system, contributed to the widening of the basis. Exporters’ inability to cancel and rebook forward contracts further exacerbated the dislocation. “Basis eased considerably on Thursday, that is, spot went up and forwards came off. However, it is still dislocated and there is further room for it to correct,” Goenka said. He added that the 94.20-94.40 per dollar range was a technically strong support zone for the currency, potentially prompting spot buying interest, particularly with Brent crude above $110 per barrel. The rupee is also facing pressure from India’s external account imbalances. An Axis Bank report said the current account deficit (CAD) was above levels that could be comfortably financed, particularly as higher global interest rates had reduced the amount of the deficit that could be funded through capital flows. “Even with new measures, CAD is well above now financeable levels,” the report said. This has kept India’s basic balance of payments in deficit for several quarters. Elevated forward premiums also point to a reversal of the covered interest parity relationship, reflecting expectations of rupee depreciation and, to some extent, pushing domestic interest rates higher, the report said. Financial outflows through overseas direct investment (ODI) have added to the pressure. RBI data showed that annualised ODI by the financial and business services sector in the current financial year so far was well above levels recorded in earlier periods. And, remittances under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme remained broadly steady. Axis Bank said measures may need to extend beyond the current account to address capital outflows. It also noted that defending the currency through higher interest rates had not proved successful in previous episodes.

item.title: Satellite lights, Google Trends can help estimate state growth: RBI report
item.description: Combining night-time illumination and Google Trends data reduced errors in quarterly growth estimates by up to 62 per cent across three industrial states ...
item.dc:creator: Anjali Kumari
item.content:encoded: Satellite-based night-time lights data and Google search trends can help estimate quarterly economic growth in Gujarat, Maharashtra and Karnataka, reducing errors in growth estimates by up to 62 per cent, according to a report in the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI’s) monthly bulletin. The report was authored by RBI staffers, and the views are those of the authors, not the RBI, it was clarified. The study, titled Nowcasting State-Level Economic Activity in India with Night-Time Light and Google Trends, combines satellite imagery and digital search behaviour to estimate quarterly growth in gross state value added (GSVA). It seeks to address gaps in the availability of timely state-level economic data, as official GSVA figures are released annually, typically with a lag of 12-18 months. The report found that combining the two indicators improved the accuracy of estimates compared with a benchmark model that relied on past GSVA growth. The reduction in the root mean squared error (RMSE), a measure of estimation error, was around 38 per cent for Maharashtra, 54 per cent for Karnataka and nearly 62 per cent for Gujarat. The framework uses night-time light data from NASA’s Black Marble satellite dataset and Google Trends indices across 25 search categories. These include searches related to jobs and education, real estate, shopping, finance, travel and automobiles. The model also incorporates past GSVA growth to generate estimates for the current quarter. Night-time light data captures changes in illumination across a state, which can reflect activity in urban settlements, industrial areas and other locations. Google search trends, meanwhile, provide a measure of digital behaviour and demand-related activity. Together, the indicators offer a more frequent view of economic conditions than annual state income data. The study found a strong relationship between year-on-year (Y-o-Y) growth in night-time light intensity and overall GSVA growth. The correlation was highest in Maharashtra at 0.90, followed by Karnataka at 0.79 and Gujarat at 0.66. The relationship remained strong and statistically significant even after the researchers excluded quarters affected by Covid. The findings suggest that satellite-based illumination can capture broad changes in economic activity, while search trends provide additional information that improves estimates. The study also found that night-time light data carried information useful for predicting subsequent GSVA growth, while Google Trends indicators contributed mainly through signals available in the same period. For the analysis, the researchers processed monthly satellite observations to remove low-quality pixels and background noise before aggregating the data into quarterly measures. They then compared changes in night-time light intensity with official state-level economic growth figures and incorporated the indicators into a statistical model to produce quarterly estimates. The study covered quarterly observations from 2013-14 to the third quarter of 2024-25 for Maharashtra and Karnataka. Gujarat’s series extended up to the fourth quarter of 2023-24 because of data constraints. The model’s performance was tested against a benchmark using an expanding-window approach, in which estimates were generated using information available up to each period. The authors also examined a modified measure of GSVA that excluded sectors such as agriculture, forestry and mining, where economic activity may not be fully reflected in night-time illumination. However, estimates for aggregate GSVA generally performed more consistently, indicating that excluding sectors with lower light intensity did not systematically improve short-term estimates. The study focuses on Gujarat, Maharashtra and Karnataka, selected as major industrial states. The authors said high-frequency regional estimates could help identify changes in economic activity and provide additional information for short-term economic assessment. The framework is intended to supplement official statistics rather than replace them. Its application beyond the three states and further improvements to the modelling approach could help assess how reliably alternative data sources can track economic activity across regions.

item.title: Britain's migration clampdown puts fear into $20 billion care sector
item.description: Roughly one-third of workers in the UK's wider adult care sector are migrants, according to the Work Rights Centre ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Lucy White In Britain, the government ensures that more than 650,000 vulnerable people receive daily visits from carers who help them wash, eat and attend to any medical conditions. That same government’s crackdown on immigration is putting the sector at risk. Roughly one-third of workers in the UK’s wider adult care sector are migrants, according to the Work Rights Centre. Around 280,000 came to the country under a Health and Care Visa between February 2022 and July 2025, a route that has since been suspended by the Labour government over fears it was being abused. Holders of the visas brought with them 429,200 dependents, many of whom also ended up working in the care sector. At the time the visa was suspended, Labour — under then-prime minister Keir Starmer — lagged far behind Nigel Farage’s far-right Reform UK in voter surveys. With migration high on voters’ concerns, the ruling party in September 2025 tasked a new home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, with introducing even greater restrictions on new arrivals as well as non-citizens already working in the UK. The government has signaled that, from July 2028, migrants will no longer be able to renew their Health and Care Visa, and instead will have to transfer to a Skilled Worker route. That carries a much higher salary requirement, and domiciliary care businesses — many of whom rely on contracts from local authorities — say they don’t get enough funding to cover paychecks of that scale.  “I will have to either downsize or just sell to a corporation,” said Shweta Maulayah, a managing director of a small care business called Maucare. “This is something that I built with passion, but I would not be able to financially keep it afloat.” The 2028 date looms large for many businesses and workers in the domiciliary care and supported living sector, which combined is worth around £15 billion ($20 billion), and their jitters are being heightened by Mahmood’s so-called “earned settlement” proposals.  Under current rules, a person arriving in Britain must stay for five years before they can apply for settlement, meaning most carers who came in 2022 and early 2023 would be eligible by the time the Health and Care Visa expires. But now Mahmood is proposing that the five-year baseline should be extended to 10 years, with reductions for high earners and those who make exceptional contributions to society through volunteering. Maulayah started recruiting from abroad in January 2023, and so has several staff who wouldn’t be eligible for settlement under those terms before the July 2028 visa deadline. “How am I going to keep them if it goes to 10 years?” she asked.Labour PoliticsPrime Minister Andy Burnham is leaning toward excluding care workers from the extension, according to a report in the Times newspaper, though it’s unclear whether the Home Office would support exemptions for people with Health and Care Visas.  Some Labour backbenchers object to the application of the new rules to people already in the country. Bloomberg reported in March that more than 100 parliamentarians signed a private letter urging the home secretary to rethink her plans. Left-leaning Labour lawmakers have made a set of demands, according to one person familiar with the matter, including that the new timelines for settlement shouldn’t be applied retroactively, that people from the same household should be able to benefit from the same timeline, and that the maximum timeline to claim settled status should be seven years. Cabinet ministers including Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh and Housing Secretary Angela Rayner have also refused to publicly back Mahmood’s reforms. Mike Tapp, a former Home Office minister who worked with Mahmood on the proposals, has also called for an exemption for care workers. During Labour’s annual conference last month the home secretary gave a first hint that she was rethinking aspects of her reforms. “I know that, throughout our consultation process, some have said elements of these reforms are not fair,” she said. “We will come to a position that balances fairness for those who came here legally and fairness to British citizens across this country.” But that might come too late for some care firms. One owner of a domiciliary care business in the south of England, who was granted anonymity discussing commercial matters, said the uncertainty has prompted her to explore options to sell her firm or wind it up. Even if exemptions from Mahmood’s reforms were introduced for care workers, she worried that current restrictions on hiring workers from abroad ultimately made her business unsustainable, as she’d find it hard to hire British staff willing to work at the pay levels her contracts with the local authority allow. Maulayah faces the same dilemma. “We’re not getting a lot of locals joining this industry,” she said. “Even youngsters that go to career fairs, they’re not that interested because they feel that care is a low-skilled job. One of them said to me, ‘I’d rather stack shelves in Tesco,’” she said, referring to the Tesco Plc supermarket chain. Back in 2022, the industry was crying out for more staff. Thousands of workers from European Union countries had left the UK following Brexit, while its aging population meant there was relentless demand.  But, following an influx from countries such as India and Nigeria, it emerged that unscrupulous care agencies were abusing the sponsored visa route. A Bloomberg investigation last year revealed that many carers who entered the UK to work in good faith were being charged tens of thousands of pounds for their visa by the business who was supposed to be sponsoring them, but that there was no job for them when they arrived in the country.  Speaking to journalists on Friday, Burnham stopped short of committing to all of Mahmood’s proposals. “We’ve been consulting on those reforms, and we will come forward with our decisions soon,” the PM said. “But I strongly support the Home Secretary when she says that settlement is a right to be earned through contribution.” Proposals are expected next month. A spokesperson for the Home Office didn’t respond to requests from Bloomberg for comment.
